lines: Picture a company where one central team still owns every single pipeline, across every business area.
The people who actually know how orders work have handed that pipeline off entirely to a team that's never touched an order. Is that genuinely the right place for that ownership to sit?
Here's the actual reversal, straight from the person who proposed it.
Instead of every team shipping its own data off to one central group for safekeeping, each business area keeps its own data and makes it available directly, on its own terms.
Here's a question worth sitting with before the next reveal.
A team now keeps and serves its own data instead of shipping it off. Does simply keeping it yourself automatically make that data something everyone else can actually rely on?
answer: Not automatically, no — reliability isn't a side effect of ownership.
Being easy to find, having a stable place to reach it, being honestly accurate, and playing well with everyone else's data are their own separate requirements a team still has to actually meet.

lines: Here's the actual shift in how that data gets treated.

A business area's own data stops being something merely extracted for someone else's use, and starts being treated the way a real product is — with the people who rely on it treated as genuine customers.
And here's exactly what being a genuine customer of that data demands.

Finding it has to be effortless, reaching it needs one stable, dependable location, trusting it means an honest guarantee about its accuracy, and combining it with other teams' data has to actually work smoothly.
Here's a harder question about what that ownership actually costs.
Every business area was already running its own day-to-day systems long before this. Does giving that same area its own data pipeline too really add any meaningful extra cost?
answer: It does add real cost, and a specific kind.

Running a day-to-day business system and running a data pipeline draw on genuinely different specialized skills. Hand every area its own pipeline with nothing shared underneath, and every one of them has to build that specialized skill from scratch.

lines: Here's that specific cost, named directly.

Spreading ownership out to every business area, with nothing shared beneath them, means every single one of them separately rebuilds the same specialized effort and skill that a shared foundation could have provided once.
Now here's the full set of ideas this approach actually rests on, named together.

Each business area owning its own data, that data treated genuinely as a product, a shared foundation that removes the need to rebuild specialized skill everywhere, and a way of keeping every area's data working together. All four, together, not any one alone.
Here's a genuinely open question worth guessing at first.

Suppose a company rolls out domain ownership, and starts treating data as a real product, starting tomorrow — but the shared foundation underneath all of it genuinely doesn't exist yet. Does the whole approach still actually work?
answer: Not yet, no — and this is exactly where it quietly breaks down.
Without that shared foundation, every single business area is left to rebuild the same specialized infrastructure skill entirely on its own, right away, with nothing shared to lean on.

lines: Here's that shared foundation's own actual reason for existing.

The specialized skill it takes to even set up this kind of infrastructure is genuinely hard to teach every single business area separately — and removing exactly that burden is the entire reason this piece exists in the first place.
Here's the piece that keeps every area's data actually working together.

Each business area keeps real freedom over its own local decisions, while a small, genuinely shared set of rules gets enforced automatically by the shared foundation itself, with no one manually signing off by hand.
Let's put the whole picture back together.
Ownership of the data moves out to each business area. Treating that data as a product is a real, specific standard, not just a phrase.
None of it is free without a shared foundation underneath it. And a shared set of automatically enforced rules is what keeps the whole thing from quietly falling apart.
One closing scenario worth genuinely thinking through.

A company rolls domain ownership and the product standard out across every team this very quarter — while the shared foundation underneath all of it is still many months away from actually being ready.
answer: Every single business area ends up paying that missing foundation's cost completely on its own, starting immediately.

The shared foundation was never meant as something nice to add on later — it was always meant to be the piece that absorbs exactly that cost, and until it genuinely exists, every area simply carries it alone.
